segments.say: Now imagine a garden in late autumn, in the soft grey light of an early evening. The trees have turned gold and copper and deep red. Many of their leaves have already fallen, and they lie in thick, soft layers on the path. The air smells of damp earth and wood smoke from a chimney somewhere nearby. Everything here is slowing down for the winter.

A small lantern glows at the edge of the path. A wooden bench waits beneath an old tree, its seat scattered with leaves. A light drizzle is falling, so fine that it feels more like a cool mist on your face. The garden is quiet. The birds have gone to roost. Even the wind seems to have settled down for the night.

Every autumn, the trees let go of their leaves. They don't hurry it, and they don't hold on. One by one, the leaves loosen and drift down, turning slowly in the air, and land softly on the ground. The tree doesn't worry about it. It knows this is simply part of resting, part of getting ready for a long, quiet winter.

Maybe you can let go a little like that tonight. The worries of the day. The tasks you didn't finish. The things you meant to say. You don't need to throw them away. You can simply loosen your grip on them, and let them drift down, slowly, to rest on the ground until morning. The tree will grow new leaves in spring. You'll find new energy tomorrow.

show.text: Letting go is part of resting.

segments.say: You walk slowly along the path, your footsteps soft on the fallen leaves. You brush a few leaves from the old bench and sit down. The wood is cool and a little damp, but your coat is warm. Above you, the branches of the tree make a dark, lacy pattern against the evening sky. Now and then, another leaf comes spinning down.

Listen to the drizzle. It's so gentle you can barely hear it. A faint whisper on the fallen leaves. A tiny patter on the lantern glass. A soft dripping from the edge of a branch. It doesn't start or stop. It just carries on, quiet and steady, like a lullaby the garden is singing to itself.

Let's gather the gentle things around you. Golden leaves, drifting down. Fine drizzle, whispering on the path. A lantern, glowing warm at the edge of the garden. An old bench, holding you up. And the faint smell of wood smoke, telling you that somewhere nearby, a fire is warm and a house is ready for the night.

After a while, you stand and walk back along the path toward a small house at the end of the garden. Its windows glow orange. When you open the door, warmth rushes out to meet you. A fire is burning low in the hearth. You hang up your damp coat, and sit down in front of the fire, letting its warmth soak slowly into your hands.

From inside, you can hear the drizzle on the roof, a little louder now, but still soft and soothing. The fire crackles gently. The room is warm and dim. Outside, the garden is getting ready for winter. Inside, you're getting ready for sleep. And both of you are doing exactly what you should be doing on a night like this.

Here's one last thought from the garden. Rest is how things grow again. The trees don't stay bare forever. After their long winter rest, they wake up full of new leaves. And you, too, will wake tomorrow a little renewed, after a long, soft night of rest. So let the garden sleep, and let yourself sleep with it.

show.text: Rest is how things grow again.

segments.say: Your body feels heavy and warm now, in front of the fire. Your eyelids are drooping. Your breath is long and slow. The sound of the rain blends with the soft crackle of the fire, until you can hardly tell them apart. And you drift, gently, a little further into rest, like a leaf turning slowly on its way down to the ground.
